shots.src: World Bank (birth rate × population) · Statistics Korea (2025)
shots.narration: In 1970, about a million babies were born in South Korea. {p} In 2023? {pp} About two hundred and thirty thousand.

shots.src: World Bank · fertility rate, births per woman (2025: Statistics Korea)
shots.narration: That year, the average Korean woman was expected to have zero point seven two children in her lifetime. {p} The lowest of any country on Earth. {pp} To keep a population stable, you need about two point one.

One of the great economic success stories of the last century, with the fewest babies of any country on Earth. {p} Korea was having about a third of the babies it needs just to stay the same size. {p} And then, last year, something nobody expected happened. {pp} The number went up. {p} Is Korea's baby crisis over? <soft>To answer that, you need to see the scariest chart in economics.</soft>

shots.src: World Bank · fertility rate; GDP per capita (current US$)
shots.narration: Korea's story actually starts with too many babies. {p} In 1960, the average woman had about six children, {p} and South Korea was one of the poorest countries on Earth: about a hundred and sixty dollars of output per person, per year. {p} The government decided families were simply too big.

shots.src: Population Reference Bureau · Korean family-planning posters, 1974 and 1980s
shots.title: The campaign
shots.narration: In 1962, Seoul launched one of the most successful family-planning campaigns in history. {p} The posters of the seventies said: sons or daughters, have two, and raise them well. {p} By the eighties, the message was blunter: even two children are too many for our crowded country.

items.text: “Sons or daughters, have two and raise them well.”

shots.src: World Bank · fertility rate, births per woman (2025: Statistics Korea)
shots.narration: It worked. {p} Too well. {p} By 1984, fertility was down to one point seven four, below replacement. {p} And it never came back. {p} One point five by the year 2000. {p} Below one in 2018. {p} Zero point seven two in 2023.

shots.src: World Bank · GDP per capita, PPP (current international $)
shots.narration: Here's the strange part. {p} In the same decades that fertility collapsed, Korea got rich. Really rich. {p} Adjusted for prices, the average South Korean now produces more than the average Japanese. {p} Korea solved being poor. {pp} Then it ran out of children.
For decades, Korea told families to have fewer children. {p} Since 2006, it has been paying them to have more. {p} For almost twenty years, the line didn't care.

shots.src: Statistics Korea (KOSTAT), via Reuters / Korea Times · marriages 2022, births outside marriage 2023
shots.narration: So why aren't Koreans having kids? {p} Start with marriage. In Korea, more than ninety-five percent of babies are born to married couples. {p} And marriage is collapsing. In 2022, about a hundred and ninety-two thousand couples got married, {p} forty-two percent fewer than a decade earlier. {p} There's even a word for young Koreans who've given up on dating, marriage and kids: the sampo generation. The give-up-three generation.

shots.src: Statistics Korea, private education survey 2024 · World Bank exchange rate
shots.narration: Then there's the cost of raising a child to compete. {p} Korean parents spend a fortune on after-school cram academies, called hagwons. {p} In 2024, private education spending hit a record twenty-nine point two trillion won. {p} That's more than twenty billion dollars, for a shrinking number of students.

shots.src: OECD · hours worked per worker, 2025 · gender wage gap, 2024
shots.narration: And then there's time. {p} Koreans work about eighteen hundred and thirty hours a year, among the longest in the rich world, {p} and at home, most of the second shift still falls on women. {p} On top of that, Korean women earn about twenty-nine percent less than men, one of the widest pay gaps in the OECD. {p} For a lot of young Korean women, it feels like a choice between a career and a child. {p} More and more, they choose the career.

Seoul is where all of this peaks. {p} About half of all South Koreans live in the greater Seoul area, {p} and in 2023, Seoul's fertility rate was zero point five five. {p} Across the country, the average mother is now thirty-three point eight years old when she gives birth. {pp} The capital is where Korea's future gets very, very small.

Here's why demographers call this the scariest chart in economics. {p} Take a hundred Korean adults. At zero point seven two, they have about thirty-six children between them. {p} Those thirty-six have about thirteen. {pp} In two generations, a hundred becomes thirteen.

shots.src: Statistics Korea (KOSTAT), via Reuters / Korea Times · 2025
shots.title: South Korea, 2025
shots.narration: And it's not a forecast. It's already happening. {p} Since 2020, more Koreans have died every year than were born. {p} In 2025: about three hundred and sixty-three thousand deaths, {p} and two hundred and fifty-four thousand births.

shots.src: World Bank (to 2024) · Statistics Korea projection (2072) · Ministry of the Interior (Dec 2024)
shots.narration: In December 2024, Korea officially became a super-aged society: one in five people is now sixty-five or older. {p} And the official projection? {p} About fifty-two million people today. {p} Thirty-six point two million by 2072. {p} And almost half of them would be sixty-five or older.

Think about what that means. {p} Fewer workers paying into pensions. Fewer soldiers. Fewer customers. {p} Schools closing, nursing homes opening. {pp} <soft>A whole country slowly turning into a retirement home.</soft>

shots.src: World Bank · fertility rate, births per woman (2025: Statistics Korea) · KOSTAT monthly births (Aug 2026)
shots.narration: And then, the twist. {p} In 2024, Korea's fertility rate went up for the first time in nine years, to zero point seven five. {p} In 2025, it rose again, to zero point eight. {p} Births jumped almost seven percent, the biggest increase since 2007. {p} And it hasn't stopped. In the first half of 2026, births were up another fifteen percent, {p} the twenty-fourth month in a row of increases.

shots.src: World Bank (birth rate × population) · KOSTAT marriages
shots.narration: Why? {p} Partly weddings. Marriages delayed by the pandemic came back, up fifteen percent in 2024 and another eight percent in 2025. {p} And partly timing: Koreans born in the early nineties, a much bigger generation than the ones after it, {p} are now in their early thirties, the peak age for having a first child.

shots.src: Korean presidential office (June 2024) · parent pay (2024) · Booyoung Group (Feb 2024) · World Bank exchange rate
shots.title: All hands on deck
shots.narration: And the country is now throwing everything at it. {p} In 2024, the president declared a national demographic emergency. {p} Parents of babies under one now get a million won a month. {p} One construction company started paying employees a hundred million won for every baby. {p} That's about seventy thousand dollars.

So, is it over? {p} Run the math again at zero point eight. {p} A hundred adults have about forty children. Those forty have sixteen. {p} Even the best month so far, June 2026, came in at zero point eight eight. {pp} Better than thirteen grandchildren. {p} Still a country that shrinks by more than half, every single generation.

shots.src: World Bank · fertility rate, births per woman (2025: Statistics Korea)
shots.narration: And Korea isn't alone. {p} The world average is now about two point two, barely above replacement. {p} Japan is at one point one five. {p} China, around one. Italy, one point one eight. {p} Even the United States is down to about one point six.

shots.src: World Bank · fertility rate, births per woman (2025: Statistics Korea)
shots.narration: So can a government fix this? {p} Hungary tried harder than most: tax breaks, cheap loans, cash for families. {p} Its fertility rate rose from about one point two to about one point six, {p} then slipped back. {pp} The only rich country comfortably above replacement is Israel, at around two point nine, {p} and demographers mostly credit culture and religion, not government checks.

Korea isn't an outlier. {p} It's a preview. {p} Most of the rich world is on the same line, just a few years behind. {pp} The question isn't whether other countries will face Korea's math. {p} It's whether anyone figures out how to beat it first.

next.title: Poland just passed Japan
next.sub: the other side of the same math

shots.narration: If you want to see what happens when a country runs this race from the other direction, watch our story on how Poland just passed Japan. {p} I'm Chartbound. See you in the next one.

yt.title: South Korea's Scariest Number Just Went Up
yt.description:
South Korea's fertility rate hit 0.72 in 2023, the lowest on Earth. Then, for the first time in nine years, it went up. How Korea went from six children per woman to under one, why young Koreans stopped having kids, the math that makes demographers panic, and whether the rebound is real.
